- **Partialling Out.** What adding a second variable actually does to the slope you already had.
- **Reading a Partial Coefficient.** What holding something fixed covers, and three variables where it goes wrong.
- **Omitted Variable Bias.** Turning the thing you could not measure into a number.

# Partialling Out

## The Two-Regressor Model for Earnings and Schooling

**The goal of this section:** say what adding a variable actually does to a
coefficient, precisely enough that you could do it by hand.

We want the return to a year of schooling once parental education is in the
model, so the model now carries two slopes rather than one:

$$
\text{earnings}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{school}_i
                  + \beta_2\,\text{parent}_i + u_i
$$

- $\text{earnings}_i$: hourly earnings of person $i$, in euro
- $\text{school}_i$: years of schooling of person $i$
- $\text{parent}_i$: years of schooling of person $i$'s parents
- $\beta_1$: the return to a year of schooling
- $\beta_2$: the return to a year of parental schooling
- $u_i$: everything else that moves earnings

<!-- IDEA 1. 10-35 min. -->

## Subscript Notation for Multiple Regressors

::: {.defn title="A convention that starts mattering today"}
Until this week there was one slope, so $\beta$ needed no subscript. There are
now two, and $\beta_1$ is not the same object as the $\beta$ of week 6 even
though both are called the return to schooling. Same name, different quantity,
different assumptions behind it.
:::

## Regression Anatomy: The Slope on the Residualised Regressor

We want an expression for $\hat\beta_1$ that we can actually read, so we ask
what part of schooling the regression has to work with:

$$
\text{school}_i = \hat\delta_0 + \hat\delta_1\,\text{parent}_i + r_i
$$

- $r_i$: the part of person $i$'s schooling that parental education cannot explain
- $\hat\delta_1$: the slope from regressing schooling on parental education

::: {.result title="Regression anatomy"}
$\hat\beta_j$ is the slope from regressing $y$ on the part of $x_j$ that the
other regressors cannot explain.
:::

## The Two-Step Residual Recipe for a Coefficient

Take those residuals and use them as the only regressor:

$$
\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_i r_i\,\text{earnings}_i}{\sum_i r_i^2}
$$

::: {.worked title="The recipe, in three lines of R"}
Regress schooling on parental education. Keep the residuals. Regress earnings
on those residuals. The slope you get back is the coefficient on schooling
from the two-variable regression, to the last decimal place.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
This is not an approximation and it is not a teaching analogy. It is an
identity, and it is what the appendix derivation shows.
:::

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Left: earnings against schooling, raw.
Right: earnings against the part of schooling that parental education cannot
explain. The right-hand slope is the coefficient from the two-variable

```

# Reading a Partial Coefficient

## The Limits of Holding Other Variables Fixed

**The goal of this section:** say what holding other things fixed does and does
not cover, and then look at three variables where adding them is a mistake.

Regression anatomy tells you what the machine did. It does not tell you
whether you should have asked it to.

::: {.caveat}
"Controlling for parental education" is a description of an arithmetic
operation. Whether that operation removes a bias, removes part of the answer,
or invents a bias out of nothing depends entirely on where the variable sits
in the story that generated the data -- and the regression cannot see that.
:::

<!-- IDEA 2. 38-63 min. -->

## Confounder, Mediator and Collider in One Causal Diagram

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Parental education causes schooling and
earnings. Occupation sits between them. Promotion is caused by both. The same
regression command does three different things to these three variables.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-1_diagram: a causal diagram, drawn not simulated. Schooling on
     the left, earnings on the right, arrow between them. Parent above with
     arrows down into both. Occupation on the arrow between schooling and
     earnings. Promotion below with arrows into it from both. Colour the
     three controls differently and label them confounder, mediator,
     collider. No model.R switch needed. -->

The taxonomy is older than the diagram convention and is set out carefully in
@cinelli2024; the collider case in particular is surveyed in @elwert2014.

## Confounders: Why Controlling Removes Bias

Parents with more schooling send their children further in school, and they
also help their children earn more for reasons that have nothing to do with
school. So schooling and earnings move together partly for a reason that is
not the return to schooling.

::: {.result}
In the population of 200,000, leaving parental education out gives 1.57. Put
it in and the coefficient is 1.30, which is the truth we wrote into the
generator.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
This is the case the phrase "adding controls" was invented for, and it is the
only one of the three where the coefficient moves toward the answer.
:::

## Mediators: Why Controlling Removes Part of the Effect

Schooling gets you into a different occupation, and the occupation pays
differently. That is not a nuisance. That is one of the ways schooling raises
earnings, and it is part of the number we said we wanted.

::: {.result}
With occupation left out, the coefficient is 1.30: the full return. Put
occupation in and it falls to 0.91. The missing 0.39 did not disappear -- it
is the part of the return that travels through occupation.
:::

::: {.caveat title="And the fallback is not safe either"}
You might say fine, report 0.91 and call it the direct effect. Even that only
works if nothing unmeasured causes both occupation and earnings. If something
does, conditioning on occupation opens exactly the problem on the next slide
[@cinelli2024].
:::

## Colliders: Why Controlling Creates a Bias

Promotion is caused by schooling and it is caused by earnings. Nothing causes
it in the other direction. Add it to the regression and something genuinely
strange happens.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Within the promoted and within the
not-promoted, the relationship between schooling and earnings is flatter than
it is overall -- and in this population it turns negative.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-1_collider: scatter of earnings on schooling for a sample of 120,
     points shaded by promotion, with the overall fit in green and separate
     fits within the promoted and the not-promoted in navy. The within-group
     lines should visibly tilt the other way. Needs B_05_04 = 0.50 and
     B_05_05 = 0.15. This is the figure students will remember, so give the
     within-group slopes on the panel. -->

::: {.result}
Leave promotion out: 1.30, the truth. Put it in: $-0.15$. The sign flips.
:::

## Why the Collider Bias Is Not Sampling Noise

Take the people who did get promoted. Some of them got there on schooling.
Some got there on earnings. So among the promoted, the ones with less
schooling must have had something else going for them -- they earned more.
Within that group, less schooling now comes with higher pay.

::: {.caveat title="Read this one carefully"}
Nothing in the world changed. Every number quoted here is computed on the full
population of 200,000, so it is not sampling noise, and it is not a bug in the
data. The correlation was manufactured by the act of conditioning. This is
the case where adding a variable made the answer worse, and it is the reason
"I controlled for everything I had" is not a defence.
:::

The general statement, and the reason post-treatment variables are the usual
culprits, is in @rosenbaum1984 and @montgomery2018.

## Why Only One Coefficient in Your Table Is Interpretable

::: {.caveat title="The other coefficients in your table"}
If you built the model to estimate the return to schooling, then the
coefficient on schooling is the one your assumptions were chosen for. The
coefficient on parental education in the same table is a different quantity
that nobody justified, and it usually cannot be read causally at all.
:::

Reporting every row of a regression table as though each were an effect is
common enough to have a name [@westreich2013], and the practice of adding
controls without saying what job each is doing is criticised directly in
@hunermund2025.

::: {.tablenotes}

# Omitted Variable Bias

## The Omitted Variable Bias Formula

**The goal of this section:** turn "but I couldn't measure everything" from a
worry into a quantity you can argue about.

We want to know how far off the coefficient is when a variable is missing, so
we compare the regression we ran with the one we wish we had run:

$$
\tilde\beta_1 = \hat\beta_1 + \hat\delta \cdot \hat\gamma
$$

- $\tilde\beta_1$: the slope on schooling from the regression that left the variable out
- $\hat\beta_1$: the slope on schooling from the regression that includes it
- $\hat\delta$: the slope on the omitted variable, in the regression that includes it
- $\hat\gamma$: the slope from regressing the omitted variable on schooling

<!-- IDEA 3. 66-92 min. -->

## Hat and Tilde: Notation for Two Estimates

::: {.defn title="Hat, and now tilde"}
A hat marks an estimate. A tilde marks an estimate from a regression that left
something out. Both are estimates; only one of them is estimating the thing you
said you wanted.
:::

## The Bias Is a Product of Two Slopes

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The coefficient with parental education
left out, as parental education is made to matter more and more. The
coefficient with it included does not move.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-1_shortlong: sweep B_05_02 (parent -> pay) from 0 to 0.60 with
     B_05_01 fixed at 0.50, and plot two lines: the short coefficient, which
     climbs from 1.30 to about 1.67, and the long coefficient, which stays flat
     at 1.30. Mark the module's headline 1.30 with a reference line. -->

::: {.takeaway}
Multiply two things and a zero anywhere kills it. A variable that moves
earnings but is unrelated to schooling costs you nothing in bias. Neither does
one strongly related to schooling that has no effect on earnings. It takes
both.
:::

## Applying the Formula to Unmeasured Ability

Ability is not in the dataset and never will be, so we cannot run the long
regression. But we can put numbers on the two ingredients and see what they
would have to be.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The estimated return to schooling as
ability is allowed to matter more. The truth stays at 1.30 throughout; only
what we would estimate moves.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-1_ability: sweep B_04_01 (ability -> pay) across a plausible
     range with B_04_02 = 0.80, plotting the short coefficient against the
     truth at 1.30. Shade the region where the estimate exceeds 1.50, which is
     roughly what the module's block 2 sample reported. -->

::: {.result}
Set ability to move schooling by 0.13 years per standard deviation and pay by
1.51 euro an hour per standard deviation. The product is 0.20, and the
estimate is 1.50 against a truth of 1.30.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Both of those are guesses, and they are guesses about the world rather than
about the data. That is not a weakness of the formula. It is the formula
telling you honestly what the argument actually turns on, and week 12 is the
week we stop being able to fix it by adding a column.
:::

## Vote: How Large Would the Ability Bias Have To Be?

Our estimate is 1.50. For the truth to be 1.00, ability would have to do two
things at once. Which pair of numbers would get you there, and would you
defend either of them out loud?

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: is the pair you chose more
or less plausible than the one on the last slide?
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.caveat title="The standing question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

[Candidate this week: every variable we controlled for is a confounder and
none is a mediator or a collider, and nothing we left out moves both schooling
and earnings. The first half is a claim about causal order that the data
cannot check. The second half has a price, and we just computed it.]

## Application

The two-slider app. One slider moves how much the omitted variable shifts
schooling; the other moves how much it shifts earnings.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote first, before anything is run: with both sliders at their midpoint, is the
estimated return above 1.30, below it, or unchanged? Then move one slider to
zero and take the vote again.
:::

Lab this week: run the three-line residual recipe on our sample and confirm you
get the multiple-regression coefficient back, then turn the collider switch on
and watch a coefficient you trusted change sign.

<!-- 97-105 min. ConcepTest 4. The second vote is the one that teaches the

## Summary: Partialling Out, Bad Controls and Omitted Variable Bias

Today was three separate ideas, each doing one job:

::: {.contributions}
1. **Partialling Out.** A coefficient is the slope on the part of a variable that nothing else in the model explains.
2. **Reading a Partial Coefficient.** Holding fixed covers only what you measured, and three kinds of variable break it in three different ways.
3. **Omitted Variable Bias.** The bias is a product of two things, so naming them turns an objection into an argument with numbers in it.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Next week: the same machinery, but the regressors stop being years and start
being categories and logarithms.
:::

## {.plain}

::: {.appendix}

## Derivation: Regression Anatomy

Show that the two-step residual recipe returns the multiple-regression
coefficient exactly.

::: {.tablenotes}
Three steps. Write the first-order conditions for the two-variable fit, use
the one for parental education to show that the residual $r_i$ is uncorrelated
with parental education by construction, and substitute. The step that does
the work is the second: it is orthogonality, and it is why the residual
carries only the schooling variation that parental education has not already
claimed. The result is the scalar version of a theorem usually stated in
matrices [@frisch1933; @lovell1963], and the short proof is @lovell2008.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]

## Derivation: The Omitted Variable Bias Formula

Show that the slope from the short regression equals the slope from the long
one plus the product of two other slopes.

::: {.tablenotes}
Three steps. Substitute the long model into the short estimator, split the
result into the long slope plus a term in the omitted variable, and recognise
that term as the auxiliary regression of the omitted variable on schooling.
The step that does the work is the third, and it is where the product
structure comes from. The same algebra with the omitted variable put back is
what week 12 uses to argue about measurement error.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]
